nodes.quote: the same needs without an optimization step: the definitive screening design.
nodes.definition: A three-level screening design of about 2k+1 runs, a folded-over conference matrix plus a centre run; main effects are clear of all second-order effects, and curvature is detectable.
nodes.note: The book now presents the DSD as a ready-made family built without an optimization step, and as a special case of the OMARS family (judging-and-comparing-designs.rst:331), not as a type of optimal design. 'Can also estimate second-order effects' overstates: all k quadratics are estimable, but the two-factor interactions stay correlated and cannot all be estimated at once (definitive-screening-designs.rst:80).

nodes.quote: then let an algorithm choose the runs that make that number as good as possible. This first
nodes.note: Still matches the book. The section now also teaches coordinate exchange (no candidate set), augmentation by the determinant of the combined information matrix, and categorical factors; see the proposed terms Information matrix and Coordinate-exchange algorithm.

nodes.quote: Mixture experiments are used to optimize recipes: the factors being varied are the proportions
nodes.note: Correct as far as it goes. The section's key assumption, that the response depends only on the proportions and not on the total amount (mixture-experiments.rst:31), could be added. The section now teaches Scheffe models, pseudocomponents and mixture-process experiments (proposed as new terms).

nodes.quote: the five quadratics apart. That single curvature signal is precisely the cue to augment the
nodes.definition: A run with every factor at coded 0. It checks overall curvature and, replicated, estimates pure error, but cannot tell which factor curves; in a factorial it keeps X orthogonal.
nodes.note: 'Tests curvature' overstates: centre runs give only a one-degree-of-freedom test for overall curvature and cannot tell the quadratics apart (comparing-design-families.rst:67). 'Without breaking orthogonality' holds for the factorial model (assessing-significance-of-main-effects-and-interactions.rst:230); in a quadratic design a centre run adds information to the intercept alone and changes its correlation with the quadratic terms (judging-and-comparing-designs.rst:280).

nodes.quote: The Pareto plot ranks the effects but leaves the cutoff to the eye;
nodes.note: Still correct for the plot itself, but out of date as a summary: the book now draws the bars coloured by sign with Lenth's margins of error as the cutoff (line 75). Add an edge from the proposed Lenth's method (ADDS_CUTOFF_TO pareto_plot).

nodes.quote: variance over the whole region. V-optimality is the closely related criterion that averages
nodes.definition: Minimize the average prediction variance over a chosen finite set of points; I-optimality, a separate criterion, averages it over the whole region.
nodes.note: The node's alias 'I-optimality' is wrong now: the book separates I-optimality (whole region) from V-optimality (finite set of points), also at judging-and-comparing-designs.rst:134. Drop the alias; I-optimality is proposed as its own term.

nodes.quote: in most systems only a few of the many effects are real, and the rest scatter around zero at the size of the experimental noise.
nodes.definition: Only a few of the many factors or effects studied are real and drive most of the variation; the rest scatter around zero at the size of the noise.
nodes.note: The current definition (main effects first, then two-factor interactions) is effect hierarchy, which the book treats as a separate principle (saturated-designs-for-screening.rst:196). The name 'Few large effects' and the DSD and Lenth sections use sparsity (definitive-screening-designs.rst:62). Drop the alias 'effect hierarchy'; Effect hierarchy is proposed as its own term.

nodes.quote: A BBD places no runs at the cube vertices: there is no run with every
nodes.definition: A three-level response surface design for the full quadratic model with no runs at the cube corners; useful when corners are unsafe, but it cannot be built sequentially.
nodes.note: Out of date: the book no longer merely names it for further research; it now has its own section (response-surface-methods.rst:345), and the OMARS section places it among the largest OMARS designs (omars-designs.rst:69).

nodes.definition: A run on one factor's axis, the others at the centre: plus or minus 1 in a face-centred design; 1.41 for two factors, 1.7 for three, in a rotatable one.
nodes.note: The fixed formula (2^k)^0.25 does not hold for the newer sections: the face-centred CCD puts axial runs at plus or minus 1 (comparing-design-families.rst:426), and the rotatable five-factor CCD on a half-fraction cube puts them at plus or minus 2 (line 428), not (2^5)^0.25 = 2.38.

nodes.quote: optimum, and the surface is bumpy, so in practice the algorithm is
nodes.definition: Point exchange: swap a design point for a candidate point whenever that improves the criterion, until no swap helps; it reaches a local optimum, so it is restarted many times.
nodes.note: 'Until the criterion is best' overstates: the book says the search climbs to a local optimum and is restarted from many random designs. The book now also teaches coordinate exchange, which needs no candidate set (proposed as a new term).

nodes.quote: For three ingredients this is a triangle,
nodes.definition: The region of allowed mixture proportions; for three ingredients a triangle, drawn as a ternary plot, with pure components at the vertices and binary blends on the edges.
nodes.note: The node restricts the simplex to three components; the book defines it as the region of allowed settings for any number of ingredients, a triangle only for three.

nodes.quote: responses are carried separately, each with its own model, and the settings are chosen with
nodes.note: Definition fine, but the topic is now taught in its own section, which compares combining into one response, the sweet spot and desirability.
